lastfm.wiki_content: Pony is the debut studio album by the English psychedelic rock band Spratleys Japs. Released in 1999 on All My Eye And Betty Martin Music, the album was a side-project of Cardiacs frontman Tim Smith and his then-partner Joanne Spratley. Although other musicians are credited as playing on the album, it is believed that this was part of an elaborate fictional conceit, and that in fact Smith and Spratley were the only musicians to have been involved with the recording. According to the history of the album presented on the All My Eye and Betty Martin website, Pony was conceived as the result of an encounter between Spratley and a displaced American bar band called The Rev-Ups (Heidi Murphy, Mark Donovan and Viv Sherrif), in a dilapidated recording studio in The New Forest. Spratley subsequently introduced Smith to the band, and work began on recording an album in the Autumn of 1998. However, as there is no apparent evidence that the band nor the studio have ever existed, the veracity of this story is in doubt. A further reference was made to the alleged New Forest studio ("Sparrow Wars") on the 2007 album Yoni by Ginger Wildheart which was produced by Tim Smith, where Smith allegedly recorded a church organ for the track "Smile in Denial". The sound of Pony was apparently inspired by a malfunctioning Mellotron that had been lent to Smith by Mellotron enthusiast Andy Thompson, and the instrument in question features on nearly every track of the album. perplexity.description:
Pony is the debut studio album by Spratleys Japs, released in 1999 and closely associated with Cardiacs frontman Tim Smith and Jo Spratley. Issued on Smith’s own All My Eye and Betty Martin Music label, it presents the group’s signature blend of psychedelic rock and pop with a homemade, cult-leaning charm, and it has come to be regarded as one of the more distinctive underground releases from Smith’s wider orbit.

The album moves between brief, fragmentary pieces and more expansive tracks, giving it a playful but carefully shaped flow. Songs such as “Fanny,” “Hazel,” and “Cabinet” showcase the band’s off-kilter melodies, quirky arrangements, and shifting dynamics, balancing whimsical pop instincts with angular rock textures. Released as the band’s only album in its original run, Pony sold in small numbers but developed a reputation as an underground cult favorite.
